1. The animation shows a grid of many houses. Each house stands for one historical scenario, and it is lit if the buyer came out ahead of the renter after ten years. Dark houses are scenarios where the renter came out ahead. The text says it uses FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac rates. It is labeled "ILLUSTRATIVE", "US only" and "history, not a forecast."

2. At first all the houses are dark. Lit houses then spread across the grid, starting at the front-left corner and filling most of it. By frame 6 most houses are lit, and a strip of dark ones remains at the back right.

3. In most of the historical ten-year windows, buying finished ahead of renting. In a minority of windows, renting finished ahead. So the answer to "does renting cost more?" is that it depends on when you buy, but in this picture buying usually came out ahead over ten years. The label says this describes the past and does not predict the future. The "ILLUSTRATIVE" tag also means the proportions may not be exact.

4. The animation gives no explicit advice. A viewer might take away that buying has usually paid off over a ten-year horizon in the US. They might also note that it doesn't always, since the dark houses show that renting sometimes wins.

5. The advice in 4 is my own conclusion. The animation only shows the lit and dark counts and the "history, not a forecast" disclaimer. It never tells the viewer to buy or rent.
